newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan test-fires two U.S. Hawk missiles.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan test-fires two U.S. Hawk missiles.

text.p: Taiwan's military on Wednesday test-fired two U.S. Hawk missiles in the Taiwan Strait, resuming live-fire manoeuvres suspended a year ago in a bid to cool down acute tensions with arch rival China.

The medium-range missiles, Taiwan's first known live-firings since the March 1996 suspension, were shot into the open sea from a base at the northern town of Tamsui, the defence ministry said in a statement.
Due to safety concerns, the test-firings halted commercial flights for two hours between Taiwan and the Taiwan-held outpost islet of Matsu just a few kilometres from China's southeastern coast.

"The missiles were nowhere near Matsu," a military source said. "But since their landing area was part of the commercial flight path between Taiwan and Matsu, we decided it would be prudent to halt flights temporarily."
Analysts say Taiwan's military manoeuvres are designed principally around the island's need to defend itself against its only adversary -- communist China.
Wednesday's drill came as China and the United States began a scheduled three-day round of talks in Beijing on nuclear technology and arms control issues.

The defence ministry said more missiles would be test fired on April 1. Taiwan said on March 4 that it would fire four U.S. Hawk missiles during the March 12-April 8 drill called Fairy Arrow Operation No.37.
Taiwan suspended its annual missile tests and other large scale drills in March 1996 to avoid exacerbating tensions with China, the island's rival since a civil war split them in 1949.
That suspension followed eight months of war games mounted by Beijing in waters near Taiwan that reached a peak in the weeks before island's historic March 23 presidential election.

China, which views Taiwan as a rebel-held province that must be brought under mainland control, mounted the war games out of fear the election was a plot by Taipei to pursue independence from the mainland rather than reunification.
Beijing has vowed to attack Taiwan if it strays from its official pro-unification policy and declares independence.
Taiwan and China have huge defence budgets.
Taiwan has asked parliament for T$260.2 billion (US$9.46 billion) for defence in fiscal 1997/98. China said it would spend 80.57 billion yuan (US$9.7 billion) on defence in 1997.

Cross-strait relations, which had warmed in the early 1990s but have been frozen since mid-1995, could take a turn for the worse on Saturday when Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, begins a six-day visit to Taiwan.
Beijing on Wednesday condemned an expected meeting between the Tibetan Buddhist god-king and Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui, accusing both of trying to "split the motherland".
